title: Declining Population Could Mean a Better Economy
paragraphs: Birth rates are falling in many countries around the world, and many people worry that this will slow economic growth. However, a new study suggests that an older, smaller population may not be as bad for the economy as many people think.

The study was written by economists Daron Acemoglu, who won the Nobel Prize in economics in 2024, David Autor, Keelan Beirne and Andrew Scott. It was published as a working paper by the National Bureau of Economic Research in the US, under the title "Baby Busts and Growth Booms."

The researchers found that, historically, lower birth rates have been linked to higher economic output per worker. For example, a 1-percentage-point lower birth rate in 1950 was associated with 23 log points higher GDP per worker in 2020, a large difference. In the United States, they also found that areas with lower birth rates saw faster wage growth.

At the same time, the researchers found no clear link between birth rates and a country's total GDP. In other words, the increase in output per worker was large enough to make up for the smaller number of workers. The authors wrote that their findings challenge the widespread pessimism about falling birth rates.

So how does this happen? According to the researchers, when workers become scarce, companies invest more in technology that reduces the need for human labor. This makes each worker more productive. Countries with lower birth rates also tended to export more high-tech products and saw faster growth in productivity.

However, the study does not mean that a shrinking population will have no problems. A smaller workforce can reduce overall demand and investment. Some countries also face very large population declines in the future. For example, the researchers note that China's working-age population is expected to fall from around 1 billion at its peak to about 300 million by 2100. It is not yet clear whether technology will be able to make up for such a large change.
